overview: Cairo was the capital of an Egyptian-centered sultanate whose military households sponsored public institutions and skilled crafts. Its political authority also extended into Syria, with different regional conquest dates.

items.text: Rulers emerged from military households whose recruits received education and training before manumission. Political advancement did not depend exclusively on hereditary succession.
Silk and spice exchange helped support artistic patronage. Egyptian textiles and carpets circulated in international markets.
Craftspeople developed enameled and gilded glass, inlaid metalwork, carved wood and textiles. Their products also influenced makers elsewhere in the Mediterranean.
Patrons endowed schools, hospitals and religious complexes. These institutions combined public services with the preservation of a patron’s name and resources.
Cairo’s buildings linked worship, education and commerce. Qaitbay’s patronage encouraged other officials to commission foundations during the fifteenth century.
The Egyptian sultanate began in 1250. Historians commonly distinguish Bahri and Burji phases around 1382; these labels do not define unchanging ethnic populations.
Tuman Bey succeeded al-Ghawri after the latter died in 1516. Ottoman conquest ended the sultanate in 1517, while Mamluk elites and artistic traditions continued under the new rulers.
